title: Wall-resolution map (y+): is the near-wall mesh right for the model?
summary: A colour map of y+ on a wall surface and a line of its span average against streamwise position, with the target band shaded. It checks that the first cell sits where the wall model expects it.

media.alt: Colour map of y plus over a wall surface above a line plot of the span average with a shaded 30 to 100 target band and a dotted segment outside the band.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the near-wall mesh right for the model?
read_the_figure.axes: Top: x/L streamwise, z/L spanwise on the wall; colour y+ from 0 to 300 (viridis). Bottom: x/L and span-mean y+ (0 to 320), with a shaded target band 30 to 100 and a one-standard-deviation band around the mean.
look_at: Where is y+ largest? Here near x/L = 0.15 and a sharp ridge at 0.8.
How much of the line lies inside the shaded band? The label says 40 percent.
Does the mean line leave the band through values too high, or too low?
Is the target band for the wall treatment actually stated (30 to 100 for wall functions)?
read_the_figure.proves: Where y+ is inside the range for the wall treatment, the first cell is in the right place for the model. It does not show the solution is right, only that the mesh is consistent with the model's assumption.
if_wrong: y+ much above the band: the first cell is in the log layer or beyond, wall functions are extrapolated.
y+ between 5 and 30 (buffer layer) with wall functions: the worst case for many models.
No band drawn: the map is colours without a criterion.

terms.meaning: Wall distance of the first cell centre in wall units, y+ = y u_tau / nu.
A model that bridges the wall layer with the log law, valid for y+ about 30 to 100 (or more).
A mesh with y+ about 1 at the first cell that resolves the viscous sublayer.
Range of y+ that the chosen wall treatment is designed for.
Mean over the spanwise direction at each streamwise position.

remember: y+ = y u_tau / nu depends on the flow, not only on the mesh: it must be checked after each run.
Wall functions: 30 < y+ < 100. Wall-resolved: y+ about 1.
The first cell may have y+ well off at stagnation and separation points.
State the target band on the plot.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Top: position on the wall surface, colour for y+ with a colour bar; contour lines mark y+ = 30 (amber) and y+ = 300 (rose). Bottom: the span-mean as a teal line, an amber band for the target, a darker teal band for the spread over the span, and a dotted rose segment where the mean is outside the band. The text states the fraction of wall inside.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Wall treatments are valid only for a range of y+, and y+ depends on the flow solution. A map shows where on the wall the criterion fails, and the line plot with a band turns the criterion into a visible region: the part of the line outside is the problem. The percentage summarises the verdict.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Where is the mesh too coarse for wall functions? Two regions rise above 100: a broad peak of about 190 at x/L = 0.15, and a ridge of about 225 at x/L = 0.8 that stretches across the span in the map. Q2: Where is y+ in the band? Between x/L of about 0.3 and 0.7 the mean is about 85 to 100, just inside (the line rides the top of the band), and at x/L = 0 near 80. Q3: Why does the label say 40 percent? It counts positions along x with the mean at or below 100: roughly 40 percent of the wall, so 60 percent is out of band and the mesh needs finer first cells over the peak regions.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Target band: the shaded region is what turns the plot from a picture into a check. Without it you cannot say where the mesh fails.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A spanwise average hides local excursions that the map shows, and the map's colours hide whether a value is 90 or 110. An average of 40 percent inside the band is a coarse summary that says nothing about where it matters most (separation, stagnation). y+ from one iteration may differ from the converged one. Target bands are conventions, not laws, and vary by model.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A histogram of y+ over the wall faces. A map of the first-cell height, which is mesh-only and does not depend on the flow. A table of y+ min, mean and max per wall.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the histogram on the right of the bottom panel and mark separation and reattachment points on the x axis.

steps.title: Friction velocity and y+
steps.note: y is the distance of the first cell centre from the wall.

steps.title: Cell height needed for a y+ target
steps.note: Because u_tau is nearly unchanged by small mesh changes, the cell height scales with the target.

worked.title: Resizing the first cell at the peak
worked.problem: At x/L = 0.8 the span-mean y+ is 225. The wall functions want y+ = 60. By what factor must the first cell height change, and what y+ does the cell have if the height is halved?
worked.answer: The cell must be 0.27 of its present height; halving it only gives 112, still above the band.

analyze.q: A map could show high y+ in a small stagnation region and low elsewhere. What would the line plot show?
What is the risk of a first cell with y+ about 10 for a wall-function model?

evaluate.q: Would you accept 40 percent of the wall in band?
evaluate.hint: Where are the other 60 percent, and what happens there?

create: Add a histogram of y+ on the wall faces and mark the fractions below, inside and above the band.
Plot the first-cell height (mesh only) next to y+ to see which part of the problem is the flow.

checks.q: Why must y+ be checked after the run?
checks.answer: u_tau comes from the solution, so y+ is known only once a solution exists.

checks.q: y+ = 150 and you want 50. Factor for the first cell height?
The map shows a ridge of high y+ at x/L = 0.8. What flow feature could be there?
checks.answer: A region of high wall shear, such as a reattachment or an acceleration, where u_tau is large and y+ is large for fixed first cell height.
